Factor Tree

DivisibilityNumber TheoryArithmetic
Game: This tool splits a number into factors until every box holds a prime number.
How to play: Press New problem, click an empty box, type one factor of the number above it and press Enter. Keep splitting until no empty boxes are left.

Look for the math

A factor tree can look different every time you factor the same number, but the primes at its ends never change. The original applet chose between 2 and 6 prime factors at random; the picker above lets you fix that number, or leave it on Random for the original behaviour.

Every split keeps the product

When a box holds N and you enter a factor a, the box beside it is filled with b = N / a. The applet only accepts that entry when a × b = N exactly. So the two new boxes always multiply back to the number above them, and the number at the very top never changes. A number like 12 may be split as 2 × 6 or as 3 × 4 — both are allowed, and neither needs to be prime yet.

The primes you end with are forced

A box that holds a prime number is finished; a composite one grows two more boxes. The unique factorization theorem says that however you choose your splits, the same primes must appear at the end, only maybe in a different order. The logic test checks every valid first factor of 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 and 60: all the finished trees print the same sorted primes, but their shapes differ. So the page is right that the tree is not unique. The closing line sorts the primes for exactly that reason.

Quick ways to spot a factor

The page suggests four divisibility rules: an even number divides by 2; if the digits add to a multiple of 3, the number divides by 3; a number ending in 5 divides by 5, and one ending in 0 divides by 10 (the page says "ends in 10"). The logic test checks all four against ordinary division for every number from 1 to 300, and they hold. They only help you find a factor — a factor that is not on these lists can still work.

GCD and LCM from the same list

Once both numbers are written as primes, the greatest common divisor takes the smaller count of each shared prime and the least common multiple takes the larger count. The test confirms this against ordinary gcd and lcm for many pairs: the page's "product of the common factors" means those shared copies, counted with repetition. One limit is worth knowing: the applet calls a number prime only if it is in its own table of primes up to 59. Its generated numbers never need a larger prime, so that never changes an answer here.

Try factoring 108 three different ways and watch the closing sentence stay the same. Then set the picker to 6 and see how much taller the tree can grow.
